title: Tales of the Steppe — Rulebook
subtitle: Story of the Steppe · year 1206 · by article

blocks.text: Tales of the Steppe (Story of the Steppe) is a turn-based strategy game set in 1206 AD — the moment Temüjin was proclaimed Genghis Khan and the peoples of the steppe upended the world. The player leads one of four great powers and seeks victory along one of five different paths (Chapter III).

It is a single-player game against AI opponents. Each year is one turn, divided into five phases (Chapter VI). The player controls provinces (villages), gathers resources, constructs buildings, recruits armies, plays cards, and conducts diplomacy and war.

This rulebook describes the game's rules exactly as implemented. Numeric values (costs, bonuses, thresholds) are binding and match the game's logic. In case of conflict the game itself is authoritative, but the goal is for this book and the game to agree.
**Province (village):** one hex tile on the map. Each province has an owner (a faction or neutral), terrain, base development, a possible trade good, and a fortification level.
**Faction:** a playable realm. Four factions are available: the Mongols, Song (China), the Rus principalities, and Khwarezm (Persia).
**Resources:** gold, food, horses, manpower, and artisans. Plus two prestige-like meters: influence and prestige.
**Influence:** diplomatic weight, generated by trade nodes, holding your capital, alliances, and Wonders. The Diplomatic Victory meter.
**Prestige:** cultural renown, generated only by Wonders (a building). The Cultural Victory meter.
**Army:** a unit stack with cavalry, infantry, and possibly siege units.
**Silk Road:** a trade route running across the map; the provinces along it are trade nodes that generate extra income and influence (Chapter VIII).
The game ends in victory when any of the following five conditions is met at the end of a player's turn. Conditions are checked at the end of every turn.
**Military Victory:** capture every enemy faction's capital — OR control at least **30 provinces** (about 40% of the map).

**Economic Victory:** three conditions at once: (a) at least **500 gold** in the treasury, (b) you control a **majority of the Silk Road's trade nodes** (more than half), and (c) you hold the gold threshold for **at least 3 consecutive turns** (the streak resets if gold drops below 500).
**Technology Victory:** play **at least 5 technology cards** (permanent tech cards).
**Diplomatic Victory:** reach **at least 100 influence** — OR form an alliance with every surviving enemy faction (at least 2 allies).
**Cultural Victory:** accumulate **at least 60 prestige** by building Wonders in your capital.
**Defeat:** the player loses if they lose all their provinces and all their armies. The AI can also win by military or economic victory, which ends the game.

The game has four factions positioned in the corners of the board: the Rus in the upper-left, the Mongols in the upper-right, Song in the lower-right, and Khwarezm in the lower-left. The center of the map is neutral.
Each faction starts with 12 provinces, a capital, and one founder army led by the Tribal Chief (Chapter XIII). Starting resources and special bonuses are listed below.

Starting relations: all factions begin neutral toward each other (relation 0, trust 50, threat 30). Exception: the others start with inherent suspicion toward the Mongols (relation −20, threat 60), since the Mongols are an aggressive expansionist power.
Starting stockpile (shared by all players): 10 food, 3 artisans, 0 influence, 0 prestige. Starting hand: 5 cards (Chapter XIV).

The map is a hex grid where every full hex contains one village. Villages are divided among the factions (edges/corners) and neutrals (center). Adjacency is computed with an odd-r hex layout: each tile borders at most six neighbors.
Terrain affects movement cost, defense, and taxation. Movement cost depends on unit type (infantry/cavalry/siege). The defense bonus adds to defender combat power (Chapter XI).
Farmland and grassland produce food; steppe and horse provinces produce horses; farmland and hills produce artisans (Chapter VII). Mountains and hills give the best defense but slow movement.
Each turn (year) proceeds through five phases in a fixed order. Move from one phase to the next with the "Next" button.
**1. Resources:** collect income from controlled provinces (gold, manpower, food, horses, artisans) plus influence and prestige. Income is calculated with the formulas in Chapter VII.
**2. Cards:** draw 1 card from the deck (the starting hand is 5) and play whichever cards you like from your hand. Card effects are in Chapter XIV.
**3. Attack:** move armies into neighboring provinces or resolve attacks against enemy- or neutral-controlled provinces (Chapter XI).
**4. Build:** construct buildings in your own provinces and recruit troops (Chapters IX–X).
**5. End turn:** the AI opponents make their moves, sieges advance, permanent bonuses update, victory conditions are checked, and a new year begins.

**Gold income** = (provinces' base tax + Silk Road bonus + market bonus + bridge bonus) × capital multiplier. A market yields +3 gold each, a Silk Road bridge +2 gold each. If the capital is lost, the multiplier is 0.5 (income halved), otherwise 1.0.
**Early-game boost:** on turns 1–4, +4 is added to gold income to speed up early construction.
**Manpower** = 30% of the provinces' combined base manpower (rounded down).
**Food** = −1 per army (upkeep) + 0.5 × farmland/grassland provinces + 2 × camps. Food can be a negative change; it is consumed by troop upkeep.
**Horses** = number of steppe/horse provinces + number of stables (1 per stable).
**Artisans** = 0.5 × (farmland and hill provinces) + number of workshops. If you control at least 3 provinces, you get at least 1 artisan per turn.
**Influence/turn** = trade nodes (1 each) + held capital (2) + alliances (2 each) + Wonders (2 each).
**Prestige/turn** = 3 × number of Wonders.

chapters.title: The Silk Road and trade nodes

blocks.text: The Silk Road is a trade route running across the map's central row. The provinces along it are trade nodes (marked with a Silk Road flag).

**Silk Road bonus** = trade nodes' base tax + 2 × nodes producing the silk trade good + **chain bonus**. The chain bonus rewards controlling unbroken runs of nodes: each connected cluster (size > 1) grants roughly 1.6 × (cluster size^1.45) extra gold. A single unbroken stretch of the Silk Road is therefore far more valuable than scattered stops.
Holding a majority of the Silk Road (more than half of all nodes) is a requirement for Economic Victory (§ 3.3) and generates significant influence (§ 7.7).
Buildings are constructed during the Build phase in your own provinces. They cost gold and often artisans. Each building grants a permanent benefit.

blocks.text: **Buildings' role in recruitment:** a Camp unlocks infantry recruitment, a Stable unlocks cavalry recruitment. In the capital, both can be recruited without a dedicated building (Chapter X).
**Wonder** is the only source of prestige and thus the key to Cultural Victory. It can only be built in the capital.
**Recruitment costs:** Infantry costs **10 gold and 5 food**. Cavalry costs **20 gold, 5 horses, and 10 food**.

**Recruitment requirements:** infantry can be recruited from a province with a Camp (or the capital); cavalry from a province with a Stable (or the capital). If the capital is lost, recruitment is suspended until it is recaptured.

**Stack composition:** an infantry recruitment produces 5 infantry (+ up to 2 cavalry depending on available horses). A cavalry recruitment produces cavalry equal to min(4 + stables, horses/2), with the remainder as infantry (at least 2).

**Movement:** an army moves into a neighboring province by paying the terrain's movement cost (Chapter V). Siege units use the siege cost; otherwise a cavalry-heavy stack (cavalry ≥ infantry) uses the cavalry cost, and infantry-heavy stacks use the infantry cost.
**Army movement:** surviving armies regain their movement allowance at the end of each turn.
**Combat power:** Attacker power = 2 × cavalry + infantry + siege + attack bonuses. Defender power = 2 × cavalry + infantry. Cavalry is thus worth double in raw power.
**Dice roll:** both sides roll 1d6. Attacker score = power + die. Defender score = power + die + 2 × terrain defense bonus + 3 × effective fortification level.
**Siege weakens walls:** effective fortification level = fortification level − 0.5 × siege units (not below 0). Siege units thus erode the defense.

**Resolution:** whoever scores higher wins. If the attacker wins, the defender takes damage (attacker power − defense bonuses); if the attacker loses, the attacker takes damage equal to the defender's power.

**Casualty allocation:** damage first hits infantry; any remaining damage removes cavalry at half effectiveness (cavalry is tougher). The defender is destroyed if it loses all its cavalry and infantry.
**Card effects:** played strategy cards can grant attack, defense, or movement bonuses, which are added to the power calculation (Chapter XIV).
**Blockade:** if a province is completely surrounded by enemy-controlled neighbors, it becomes besieged and the siege gauge grows turn by turn.
**Effect of siege:** if the province has a fortress, its level drops by −1/turn under siege. If there is no fortress, the owner loses 5 gold/turn. The siege gauge resets once the blockade is lifted.
**Lost capital:** if your own capital is in enemy hands, (a) all gold income is halved (§ 7.1) and (b) recruitment is suspended (§ 10.2) until the capital is recaptured.
**Enemy capitals** are the key to Military Victory: capturing every enemy capital ends the game in victory (§ 3.2).
Every faction founder army (the main army) carries the Tribal Chief, who provides a leadership bonus.
**Death of the Chief:** when the player founder army is destroyed, a one-time penalty follows: **−30 gold** and **−15 influence**. This happens only once.
Protecting the Chief is therefore strategically important: don't send the founder army into needless risks early on.
**Drawing cards:** the game starts with a 5-card hand; during the Cards phase you draw 1 new card per turn. Played cards go to the discard pile (except permanent technology cards).
**Card types:** strategy (combat bonuses), technology (permanent bonuses; 5 played = Technology Victory), diplomacy (relations), and resource (gold/food/horses/artisans).
**Rarities:** common, uncommon, rare, legendary. Rarer cards are more powerful but appear less often.

**Duration of effects:** resource cards take effect immediately (gold/food/horses/artisans are added to stockpiles). Attack/defense bonuses last a set duration (often just this turn); a movement bonus adds movement points immediately. Permanent attack/defense cards (technology) remain in effect for the rest of the game.
Cards appear illustrated in the card panel at the bottom of the game view. The panel can be enlarged or shrunk by dragging its top edge; cards always scale to stay fully visible.
**Relations:** every pair of factions has a relation score, trust, threat, and border friction. Treaties change these values.
**Treaty types:** peaceful — non-aggression, peace, truce, and alliance; and war-related — formal war (war_formal) and surprise attack (war_surprise).
**Alliance** generates +2 influence/turn (§ 7.7). An alliance with every surviving enemy (at least 2) is one path to Diplomatic Victory (§ 3.5).

**Declaration of war:** a formal war activates on a set turn and crashes relations (−90) and trust (0), and raises threat (+30). The Mongols already carry a higher starting threat from the outset (§ 4.3).
Some provinces produce a trade good, which grants a permanent benefit to its owner. Value describes the good's relative worth in trade.

At the end of a turn, each AI faction acts according to its personality: the aggressive one (Mongols) expands and attacks, the merchant (Song) focuses on the economy, the defensive one (Rus) fortifies, and the expansionist (Khwarezm) takes neutral provinces.
The AI can win by military or economic victory under the same conditions as the player. AI moves are shown in the end-of-turn notifications.
The AI takes threat and relation scores into account: high threat increases the likelihood of attack. The Mongols' high starting threat makes them a likely aggressor.
**Use the early-game boost:** on turns 1–4 you get +4 gold/turn. Build markets and camps early as the foundation for your economy and recruitment.
**Hold the Silk Road in one unbroken stretch:** the chain bonus (§ 8.2) rewards adjacent trade nodes disproportionately — build one unbroken run instead of scattered stops.
**Protect your capital and your Chief:** a lost capital halves income and halts recruitment; the death of the Chief costs 30 gold and 15 influence.

**Choose your victory path early:** for the Mongols the military path is natural (cavalry +30%), for Song the economic and cultural path (taxation +30%), for Khwarezm expansion, and for the Rus a defensive war of attrition.
**Use terrain:** defend in mountains and hills (+3/+2 defense), attack with cavalry in open terrain where movement is cheap.
**Siege units against walls:** bring siege units against fortified provinces — they weaken the effective fortification level (§ 11.3).
